value.text: Just weeks before a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 claimed the life of a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective, state records uncovered by WPTV reveal that the Florida Department of Transportation announced a $54 million interchange improvement project that includes technology designed to prevent similar tragedies.The project, announced Nov. 4, includes the installation of wrong-way driver detection systems on I-95 exit ramps in Palm Beach County, including near the area where Detective Alan Smith was killed Thanksgiving morning.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The Florida Highway Patrol said Smith, 46, was driving south on I-95 just north of Military Trail shortly after 5 a.m. Thursday when an intoxicated driver traveling in the wrong direction collided with him head-on.WPTV has not yet determined which ramp the driver used to enter I-95 or whether the planned technology could have prevented Thursday's deadly crash.However, FDOT records detail how the technology is designed to work.According to FDOT, the moment a driver enters an exit ramp in the wrong direction, radar detectors and cameras detect the vehicle, triggering flashing red LED "WRONG WAY" signs intended to prompt the driver to stop and turn around.The system also captures images of the vehicle and sends alerts to transportation management centers and the Florida Highway Patrol.As troopers work to intercept the wrong-way driver, electronic message boards along the interstate can warn other motorists of the approaching danger.At least seven locations along I-95 in Palm Beach County are slated to receive the technology:Northbound exit ramp at Blue Heron BoulevardNorthbound and southbound exit ramps at Palm Beach International AirportNorthbound and southbound exit ramps at Forest Hill BoulevardNorthbound and southbound exit ramps at 10th Avenue NorthNorthbound and southbound exit ramps at Atlantic AvenueNorthbound exit ramp at Linton BoulevardNorthbound and southbound exit ramps at Palmetto Park RoadThe $54 million project is part of a broader statewide effort to combat wrong-way driving. FDOT also plans to install additional roadside warning signs and pavement markings.Florida Highway Patrol data shows more than 3,800 wrong-way crashes were reported statewide in 2024 alone, 105 of which were fatal.Smith's death comes just one month after another deadly wrong-way crash on I-95 in West Palm Beach killed one person and seriously injured two others.Construction on the interchange improvement project is scheduled to begin this month, with completion expected in 2029.WATCH BELOW: PBSO detective killed by drunk wrong-way driver on I-95, FHP saysAs WPTV previously reported, troopers identified the driver accused of causing Thursday's deadly crash as Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens.Investigators said Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash and was driving despite three prior DUI convictions and an active 10-year driver's license revocation.Smith, who was on duty and headed to work in an unmarked patrol vehicle, was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.Espinoza Martinez was hospitalized with serious injuries and arrested Thursday afternoon.Members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office joined troopers at the hospital, placing Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective, according to FHP.Troopers said Espinoza Martinez would be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail upon his release from the hospital on multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide and aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer.A judge on Friday ordered Espinoza Martinez to be held on a $1.7 million bond.President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel paid tribute to Smith on Thursday.Smith served nearly 20 years with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and specialized in explosives-related investigations, according to Patel.He graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013 and served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives."This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe," Patel wrote on X. "Never forget them and their families."Smith leaves behind a wife and 14-year-old son.The Florida Highway Patrol continues to investigate the circumstances surrounding the crash.

A judge set a combined $1.7 million in bonds Friday for the man accused in a deadly Thanksgiving morning crash that killed a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective.Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, was scheduled to make his first court appearance Friday but was unable to attend because he remains hospitalized.WATCH REPORT BELOW: According to court records, Judge Autumn Gurrola waived Espinoza Martinez's first appearance, found probable cause for the charges against him and established bond amounts and conditions.Espinoza Martinez faces eight charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide and aggravated battery, in connection with the crash that killed PBSO Detective Alan Smith.Court records show Gurrola set a $1 million bond for vehicular homicide, $500,000 for driving with a suspended license causing death or serious bodily injury, $100,000 for DUI causing property damage or injury and another $100,000 for reckless driving causing property damage or injury.The judge granted release on recognizance for three additional charges, including two aggravated battery counts and driving with a suspended or revoked license.Release on recognizance means a defendant does not have to post a monetary bond for those particular charges but must comply with court-ordered conditions.No bond was listed for the DUI manslaughter charge.Despite the $1.7 million in monetary bonds, Espinoza Martinez's release remains subject to a pretrial detention order.During Friday's hearing, prosecutors requested pretrial detention, which would allow the court to keep Espinoza Martinez in custody while his criminal case moves forward.Court records show the judge granted the motion to schedule a pretrial detention hearing and that an order granting pretrial detention was filed.A pretrial detention hearing is expected to take place within five days.The court also established several conditions that would apply if Espinoza Martinez is released.Those conditions include:House arrest with monitoring by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.No contact with Smith's next of kin.No driving.No alcohol, illegal drugs or nonprescription drugs, with random testing.Surrendering all passports and travel documents to the clerk's office within 24 hours of release.During Friday's court proceedings, prosecutors also revealed that Espinoza Martinez was still on probation for his third DUI conviction at the time of the deadly crash.According to investigators, Espinoza Martinez was driving the wrong way on Interstate 95 while intoxicated when he crashed into Smith's vehicle Thanksgiving morning.Smith, a nearly 20-year veteran of PBSO, was on his way to work when the crash happened.Investigators say Espinoza Martinez had three previous DUI convictions and was driving with a revoked license.Court records show Espinoza Martinez is scheduled for a 30-day return hearing on Dec. 26 at 10:30 a.m. at the Palm Beach County Criminal Justice Complex on Gun Club Road.An initial case conference is also scheduled for Jan. 21, 2027, at 8:30 a.m. at the main courthouse in downtown West Palm Beach.The date of his pretrial detention hearing was not specified in the court event form.Espinoza Martinez remains hospitalized, and it is unclear when he will be able to appear in court.

This week's heavy rainfall left behind flooding across parts of Palm Beach County, and one of downtown West Palm Beach’s most recognizable holiday traditions also took a hit.Sandi, the city's massive holiday sand tree, is showing visible damage after the recent rain.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Collapsed sections of sand, divots, and partially buried lights could be seen on the tree as families stopped by downtown West Palm Beach. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with the Fox family. Their son says he is very sad about Sandi."I hope that they fix the sand tree. I am so sad that it got hit by the weather and rain," he said.For the Fox family, visiting Sandi is something they look forward to each holiday season."One of the things we love about Florida is we get to celebrate the holidays with the warm weather. We don't get snow, but we get the Sandi tree. Unfortunately, with all the rain, it's not looking too good," Asia Fox said.The family said seeing Sandi has become an annual tradition.Now, they and others are waiting to see how quickly the damage can be repaired and whether it could affect the tree lighting scheduled for Dec. 3.WPTV reached out to the city of West Palm Beach about the damage. The city said it will continue to assess Sandi and will provide updates if there are any changes to the tree-lighting schedule.

Holiday shoppers took to the stores en masse on Black Friday, the traditional day after Thanksgiving, to start on holiday gift lists and look for discounts. At the Tanger Outlets in West Palm Beach, Rich Paul-Hus had three shopping bags from the Le Creuset store. "It was 30% off," Paul-Hus told me. Another shopper named Lisa had bags from the New Balance store. "Five pairs of shoes, $120," Lisa said. "We have over 120 stores," says Alexis Araujo, marketing director for Tanger Outlets Palm Beach. "Here's a little bit of a pro tip: if you download our Tanger app, it's free, you get 15 to 25% off on top of all the discounts that are already existing," Araujo said.Finding bargains can take some work. "Don't go into any sales event without a plan; that's what leads to impulse purchases," budgeting expert Andrea Woroch said. She outlined how shoppers can use artificial intelligence to snag the best deals."You can use ChatGPT or Google Gemini and ask some simple prompts," she says. "Enter the product name, ask the tool to compare prices." Woroch said as a general rule, 30% off is a good benchmark for a good deal. One thing shoppers need to avoid this holiday is using credit cards. Experts say it's wise to use them only if you're paying off the purchases in a month, and avoiding the interest rates above 20%. "Enjoy the holiday season, enjoy the time with family and friends," Ted Rossman of Money Management International said. "Stick to a budget, don't go into expensive debt that's going to make it that much harder to pay it off."More Black Friday coverage below:

Nearly a month after historic flooding forced families from their homes in Martin County, displaced residents now have another option for temporary housing — at no cost.Martin County announced that residents can apply for temporary RVs or travel trailers through EmergencyRV, a nonprofit organization that partners with disaster response and recovery agencies to provide housing to eligible disaster survivors.The assistance comes after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some Jensen Beach homes earlier this month. According to county estimates, at least 36 homes sustained damage, resulting in approximately $3 million in residential losses.The RVs and travel trailers, most of which are loaned to residents, can be placed on homeowners' properties where feasible, allowing families to remain close to their homes while repairs or reconstruction are underway.According to Martin County's website, residents are encouraged to apply if they:Have been displaced as a direct result of the flooding.Sustained damage that prevents them from safely occupying their homes.Have an unmet temporary housing need while pursuing a permanent housing solution.Have a suitable location for an RV with access to, or the ability to establish, water, electricity, and sewer or septic connections.Residents can apply directly through EmergencyRV here.The nonprofit advises applicants to allow up to seven days for a response. That does not guarantee placement within seven days.Assistance is subject to eligibility, site feasibility, and resource availability.It remains unclear what options are available to displaced residents whose properties cannot accommodate an RV or the necessary utility connections.The announcement follows weeks of WPTV reporting on the challenges displaced families face in securing financial assistance and temporary housing.Earlier this month, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading with elected officials for immediate help.Among them was Lisa French, a Jensen Beach mother of two whose home sustained several inches of flooding. Water remained inside her home for more than a week, causing mold to grow several feet up the walls."We just need somebody to step up," French previously told WPTV. "We need funding."Martin County commissioners approved financial assistance through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program, including grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.However, the grants are reimbursement-based, requiring homeowners to pay for eligible repairs upfront. Income restrictions could also leave some families without assistance.On Nov. 20, WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey pressed Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Jared Perdue on what immediate relief the state could provide to displaced families."What can you promise them right now, not weeks from now, about the help that's coming?" Hussey asked."Well, we're committed. We're fully mobilized," Perdue responded.Perdue also pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations to assist flood victims with recovery efforts."Our goal is to, you know, meet the needs that are out there and make sure we help people get back on their feet as quickly as possible," Perdue said.The temporary housing opportunity comes just days after President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a major disaster declaration following weeks of uncertainty over whether federal assistance would become available.The state submitted an expedited disaster declaration request Nov. 9.Late Tuesday, FEMA announced federal disaster assistance was available to individuals and families in six Florida counties: Martin, Palm Beach, St. Lucie, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard.That assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-interest loans to cover uninsured property losses, and other disaster recovery programs.Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to eligible local governments for debris removal and emergency protective measures.Martin County previously estimated approximately $18 million in residential, beach, and roadway damage, not including additional emergency response expenses.Residents seeking temporary housing through the EmergencyRV website. Residents seeking federal disaster assistance should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance on the agency website, through the FEMA app, or by calling 800-621-3362.Additional recovery resources are available on Martin County's disaster recovery website.

While many families gathered around the dinner table Thursday, Bill Caesar spent his Thanksgiving making sure those without a table to gather around weren't forgotten.Inside a Delray Beach home, about 40 volunteers worked together to pack 350 plates of hot food, complete with turkey, mashed potatoes and string beans.It's a Thanksgiving tradition Caesar has carried on for about 15 years through his charity, Coming Back to Give Back.WATCH: More than a meal: Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need"I got here at 4 o'clock this morning," Caesar said.For thousands of Floridians, Thanksgiving looks vastly different from the holiday many have come to know. More than 24,000 people are experiencing homelessness statewide, including more than 1,500 in Palm Beach County alone. Others face financial hardship, isolation or limited mobility.Caesar wants to make sure those circumstances don't keep anyone from enjoying a Thanksgiving meal."It's a great feeling whenever you can give back," said Caesar. And for those who can't come to him, he goes to them.One of his stops Thursday was Lakes of Delray, a senior living community where he delivered 50 meals to residents, some of whom have difficulty leaving their homes or don't have family nearby."Can’t get around, so we're bringing it to them," Caesar said.From there, Caesar headed to a bus station, where he delivered a Thanksgiving dinner to a woman named Pauline, who has recently fallen on hard times."Special delivery!" Caesar said as he approached her.He handed her a plate of food, checked on her, and wished her a blessed Thanksgiving.Throughout the day, Caesar did more than distribute meals. He introduced himself, struck up conversations and connected with people throughout the community.For Caesar, the food is a way to offer something more: human connection."It's a great day brightening everybody else's day and making sure everyone's good," Caesar said after sitting and talking with a man named Willie. "He was like, ecstatic; he was like, 'Oh my god, I didn't have a meal, I didn't know what I was going to do today." On a holiday centered around togetherness, even a brief conversation can carry meaning for someone accustomed to being overlooked.For people like Willie, Anthony and Jamie, whom Caesar visited Thursday, the greatest gift of Thanksgiving may not be what's on the plate, but the reminder that someone cares.Because sometimes, it's not just about having a place to get a meal.It's about feeling like you have a place in the world.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Black Friday shoppers were out early across South Florida on Friday, with some music fans waiting for hours to get their hands on limited-edition vinyl releases.About 80 people lined up outside Rust & Wax record store in West Palm Beach as shoppers sought special limited-edition Record Store Day releases from artists including The Beatles, Cher, Sombr, the Grateful Dead and Stevie Nicks.WATCH REPORT BELOW:T.A. Walker caught up with Diane of Palm Beach Gardens, a Stevie Nicks fan who arrived around midnight and scored one of the records on her wish list. She was among the first customers inside the store Friday morning and had her sights set on a special Stevie Nicks release of "Bella Donna.""She took the face of the 'Bella Donna' album and imprinted it directly on the actual album itself," Diane told Walker. "So when you're listening to 'Bella Donna,' you're actually seeing Stevie Nicks."The early-morning rush wasn't limited to record collectors.Shoppers were also heading to retailers and shopping centers across the area, including Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Macy's, Kohl's, The Mall at Wellington Green, The Gardens Mall, Town Center at Boca Raton and Treasure Coast Square.The crowds come as many consumers still plan to do at least some of their holiday shopping in person.According to holiday shopping research cited by Accenture, 66% of consumers plan to hunt for Black Friday or Cyber Monday deals at brick-and-mortar stores rather than doing all of their shopping online.The research also found the average consumer is expected to spend about $737 this holiday season.For the music fans waiting outside Rust & Wax, however, Black Friday was about more than simply finding a discount. It was a chance to be among the first to grab a limited-edition release before it disappeared from the shelves.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel are paying tribute to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective killed in a Thanksgiving morning wrong-way crash on Interstate 95.Speaking in Palm Beach on Thursday, Trump offered his condolences to the fallen detective's family."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, an expert at bombs and explosives, who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty," Trump said.Authorities have since identified the fallen detective as Alan Smith, 46, of West Palm Beach.Trump did not identify Smith during his remarks Thursday, citing ongoing efforts to notify his family and others.In a statement posted on X, Patel revealed Smith had served nearly 20 years with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and had extensive experience investigating explosives-related crimes.Smith graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013 and served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, according to Patel."This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe," Patel wrote. "Never forget them and their families."Smith leaves behind a wife and 14-year-old son.The Florida Highway Patrol said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol vehicle south on I-95 just north of Military Trail shortly after 5 a.m. Thursday, when a driver traveling in the wrong direction collided with him head-on.Smith was on duty and headed to work at the time of the crash, according to the sheriff's office. He was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.Troopers identified the wrong-way driver as Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens.Investigators said Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash and was driving despite three prior DUI convictions and an active 10-year driver's license revocation.Trump also addressed the circumstances surrounding the deadly collision."It was a drunk driver — really drunk driver," Trump said. "He was going on the opposite side of the highway, if you can believe it. And so it's a terrible thing that happened."Espinoza Martinez was hospitalized with serious injuries and arrested Thursday afternoon.Members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office joined troopers at the hospital, placing Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective, according to FHP.Troopers said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail upon his release from the hospital on multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide and aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer.The Florida Highway Patrol continues to investigate the crash.

Alan’s legacy of service, knowledge, compassion, and dedication to others will never be forgotten.— PBSO (@PBCountySheriff) November 26, 2026 The sheriff's office said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol car at the time of the crash. Espinoza Martinez was also taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries.All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours.The Florida Highway Patrol said at about 2:33 p.m., troopers arrested Espinoza Martinez in connection with the fatal wrong-way crash. The arrest took place at St. Mary's Medical Center, according to FHP."Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective," FHP said in a statement.A judge on Friday ordered Espinoza Martinez to be held on a $1.7 million bond.According to FHP, Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash, with an active license revocation for 10 years and three prior DUI convictions.Upon his release from the hospital, FHP said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on the following charges:Vehicular HomicideDUI ManslaughterAggravated BatteryAggravated Battery on a Law Enforcement OfficerDriving While License Suspended or Revoked Causing Death or Serious Bodily InjuryDriving While License Suspended or Revoked – Subsequent OffenseDUI Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonReckless Driving Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonFHP said they are investigating the circumstances of the crash.President Donald Trump made a statement about the crash during a press conference on Thursday, according to CNN."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, uh, an expert at bombs and explosives who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty, and I'm not able to release his name yet. They, they're notifying the family and notifying a lot of people.

Before South Florida families sit down for Thanksgiving dinner, a local doctor says a few food safety precautions involving the turkey, kitchen and leftovers can help prevent an unwanted guest at the holiday table: food poisoning.WPTV's Michael Hoffman sat down with Dr. Kleper De Almeida an infectious disease specialist at Good Samaritan Medical Center to break down what people should know as they prepare Thanksgiving dinner and plan for the leftovers that follow."The concern is of salmonella," de Almeida said.His advice starts before the turkey ever reaches the oven.De Almeida told WPTV that a frozen turkey should be thawed in the refrigerator or using cold water.Keeping raw poultry from contaminating other ingredients and kitchen surfaces is an important part of the process.Current USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service guidance emphasizes keeping raw poultry separate from foods that will not be cooked and cleaning hands, utensils and surfaces throughout meal preparation. [fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida also cautioned against washing a raw turkey because water that touches the bird can contaminate the sink and surrounding areas."Heat from the cooking process is sufficient to kill the bacteria," de Almeida said. "Washing the bird is OK, but you have to keep in mind that the water that has touched the bird can contaminate the sink."When it comes to determining whether Thanksgiving turkey is safe to eat, temperature matters."Cooking the poultry at a temperature that exceeds 165 is sufficient to prevent the risk of salmonella infection and other infections," de Almeida said.The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service says turkey should reach a minimum internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, measured with a food thermometer in the thickest part of the breast, innermost part of the thigh and innermost part of the wing. [fsis.usda.gov]If stuffing is cooked inside the turkey, the center of the stuffing should also reach 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]Once Thanksgiving dinner is finished, food safety doesn't stop.Hoffman asked de Almeida how long people should keep digging into their Thanksgiving leftovers."Three days," de Almeida said. "So they have cooked the food on Thursday. They have Friday, Saturday, Sunday to get done with what was served."For additional context, federal food safety guidance gives a slightly broader window. The USDA advises refrigerating perishable leftovers within two hours and eating or freezing refrigerated Thanksgiving leftovers within three to four days. That makes the Monday after Thanksgiving the federal guidance's use-or-freeze deadline. [foodsafety.gov], [fsis.usda.gov]Leftovers should be reheated to an internal temperature of 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida advised people who are pregnant or immunocompromised to be particularly cautious with Thanksgiving leftovers."Women who are pregnant and immunocompromised people, they need to be extra cautious," de Almeida said. "And the rules for leftovers are more stringent, so they should consume the leftovers within one day."Food safety is especially important when preparing a large holiday meal with multiple dishes moving in and out of the refrigerator, oven and serving area.So while Thanksgiving is about good food, family and friends, keeping an eye on how that food is prepared, cooked, and stored can help ensure the holiday memories don't include a bout of food poisoning.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two Palm Beach County home-based baking businesses are turning a love of baking into neighborhood side hustles, using social media to connect with customers without opening traditional storefronts.WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache first noticed the small bakery stands appearing on her own TikTok feed. She connected with Sweet Marie’s in West Palm Beach and DynastyDough in Boca Raton to learn how the entrepreneurs behind them are building businesses from home.WATCH: Palm Beach County home bakers build businesses through social mediaA mother-daughter business in West Palm BeachAlong Florida Avenue in West Palm Beach, Nicola Billows and her mother, Celina Billows, operate Sweet Marie’s.The two told WPTV they both have full-time jobs. “So I was like, mom, let’s make this come to life.”Before opening their stand, the pair said they distributed hundreds of free samples throughout their neighborhood. Customers can now stop by their Florida Avenue stand Monday through Saturday.Celina Billows said balancing the bakery with her career can be demanding.“It’s definitely a challenge to balance both my job and then baking, but you know what, we make it work,” she said.For her daughter, the business offers another kind of benefit.“My job can be, like, very heavy and overwhelming most nights, so this is just such a good outlet,” Nicola Billows said.Operating a small neighborhood stand also requires trust. Sweet Marie’s uses an honor system, which Celina Billows said has left her encouraged by the community’s response.“I have had my faith restored in humanity,” she said. “There are so many wonderful people, and we are on an honor system and, like, every day, we’re amazed.”A few miles away, another baker is finding his own community of customers.DynastyDough grows in Boca RatonAlong Northwest 35th Lane in Boca Raton, Peyton Ming operates DynastyDough while also working full-time as a Realtor.Ming told WPTV he has baked since he was young. He built his bakery stand using recycled materials given to him by people in the community.“What better way to connect with the community than to sell bread in the community?” Ming said. “I just think that food and good bread in general brings people together.”DynastyDough offers items including bread, muffins and bagels, with pre-order pickups available on Fridays.Ming said the response after promoting his business on social media caught him by surprise.“I had so many people come by on the very first week, and I was shocked,” he said.Florida cottage food law allows home-based businesses to operateHome-based food businesses such as these operate under rules established by Florida law.Under Florida’s cottage food law, a qualifying cottage food operation is exempt from the state's food permitting requirement if it follows the law and does not exceed $250,000 in annual gross sales of cottage food products. The law also allows cottage food businesses to sell and accept payments online, but prohibits wholesale sales. Florida law includes additional requirements governing eligible cottage food operations and product labeling.For entrepreneurs such as Ming, running a business from home allows work and community to intersect.“Of course, it’s still a job, but it feels much more real life when I’m able to connect with the community and do it from the comfort of my own home and my own neighborhood,” he said.Neither business owner knows exactly where the venture will take them. For now, they are continuing to bake, post on social media and build their customer bases one order at a time.Asked what he would tell someone who has an idea but is hesitant to pursue it, Ming offered advice from his own experience.“You can do something and start something scared and learn along the way,” he said. “That’s something that I really fall back on every time, and I think about how far I’ve come.”Where to find themSweet Marie’s is located at 1211 Florida Ave., West Palm Beach, FL 33401. For updates on availability and bakery stand information, follow Sweet Marie’s on Instagram. For DynastyDough pickup and location information, visit DynastyDough on TikTok. The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is investigating multiple overnight vehicle burglaries in the Lakewood Park area after surveillance video showed two people entering unlocked cars. The incidents were reported along Lakeland Boulevard, North Boulevard, Coquina Boulevard, Deleon Avenue and Paso Robles Boulevard, deputies said. Surveillance footage from one location shows two people walking onto a driveway, opening unlocked car doors and entering vehicles. The sheriff’s office said there were no broken windows or signs of forced entry. Photos released by the agency show suspects using a credit card stolen during the burglaries. One image shows what a suspect was wearing during the incidents, according to the sheriff’s office. See also: Man accused of killing PBSO deputy in Thanksgiving crash held without bond, on ICE hold Anyone who recognizes the people shown in the video or photos, or has information about the burglaries, is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at 772-462-7300. The sheriff’s office recommends removing valuables and keys from vehicles and locking car doors.

The City of Stuart is warning local businesses and contractors about a fraudulent email scam involving fake invoices for development, building, planning, or project-related fees. According to the City, several businesses with active projects and applications have recently reported receiving emails claiming to be from the City of Stuart and requesting thousands of dollars in fees. In some cases recipients were instructed to wire funds. The City says it does not send invoices by email for these purposes, and that all official City development and permitting fees must be paid through the City’s official OpenGov application portal. One of the fraudulent email addresses reported to the City is: commissions.stuartfl.gov@usa.com. The City encourages applicants with active projects to remain vigilant and carefully review all correspondence related to their projects to prevent getting scammed.

Another round of heavy rain in Florida is once again raising concerns about flooding and flood insurance. According to the Insurance Information Institute, as much as 80% of Florida homeowners don't carry flood insurance, even though just one inch of water in a home can cause $25,000 in damage.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "Everyone is in a flood zone," says Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth Rindom Insurance in Stuart. "It's just a matter of if you're in a high risk or a low risk." He said many pass on the coverage because of costs, being in a low-risk zone and also not fully understanding their homeowners policy. "If a hurricane comes and creates a flooding event, they think I have hurricane coverage," he said. But those claims are often denied since homeowners policies only cover wind damage. Experts say relying on FEMA in flood situations can leave homeowners short, since FEMA grants will cover temporary housing and essential repairs. National flood insurance will cover $250,000 on the structure and $100,000 on the contents of a home. Costs for flood insurance can vary from $600 to $1,300 a year. In addition to national flood insurance, there are also options for flood insurance with private insurers, and there are waiting periods before policies become active.

Millions of people are hitting the road this Thanksgiving holiday, but getting to their final destination isn't always going according to plan.Heavy rain moved across South Florida on Wednesday, adding another challenge for drivers traveling to spend the holiday with family and friends.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE HERE: Even with rain in the forecast, some travelers weren't prepared for the unexpected delays they encountered along the way.More than 4.2 million Floridians are expected to travel by car for Thanksgiving, according to AAA. Nationwide, the Federal Aviation Administration also expects more than 417,000 flights during the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period, making it the busiest Thanksgiving travel stretch in 16 years.For many travelers, the goal was simply getting home."I haven't been home in like a month and a half," one traveler said.Others were making their way to South Florida, including one man who said, "We're trying to get to Miami."But the journey became more complicated for drivers on Florida's Turnpike in Palm Beach County.A jackknifed tractor-trailer shut down the southbound lanes, leaving drivers stuck in standstill traffic. The delay was an unexpected hurdle for people already navigating wet roads and holiday congestion.One man making the trip from Georgia to Miami was among those caught in the backup. Another traveler said a drive that typically takes two hours had quickly turned into three."We knew it was going to rain today all day long," one driver said.Another woman said she expected some delays because of the weather but was surprised by how long traffic had come to a stop."Well, we didn't expect to be sitting here an hour for sure. We expected some delays because of rain and potential flooding," she said.The delay was so significant that she was considering changing her plans altogether."We actually might, because it's been so long, might turn around and go back to my daughter's house, in West Palm Beach," she said.Others found ways to make the unexpected wait a little more entertaining. Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding.FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue.U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding.The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster.Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App.Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying.Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties.Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide — nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs.Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments.What residents should do:File a claim with their insurance provider.Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362.Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, are in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office says a 17-year-old heard a suspicious noise outside his family's home in Palm City's Evergreen Club, prompting a 911 call and an extensive overnight search. Investigators say the group parked a vehicle near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community and targeting a home. Deputies later recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm during their investigation.WATCH: Teen's Alert Leads to 4 Arrests After Palm City ManhuntThe sheriff's office is now asking residents in the Evergreen Club community to check their homes, vehicles and security cameras for anything suspicious as investigators try to determine why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Martin County and whether any other properties were targeted.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when the family's 17-year-old son realized something was wrong."The 17-year-old son heard a noise, woke up, knew something was wrong, but didn't quite know what it was," Budensiek said. "(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house."Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen.The family called 911.Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal."There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said.The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood.One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff.Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt."The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted."We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night."The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in.Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City.MORE PALM CITY: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki CamerlengoThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A homeowner's quick call to 911 helped interrupt an attempted home invasion in Palm City early Tuesday, leading to the arrests of four people from Jacksonville, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.The sheriff's office said the homeowner heard a noise outside a home on Southwest Bimini Circle in the Evergreen Club and contacted authorities. A Port St. Lucie man has been sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate a popular online streamer as part of a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that authorities say cost victims about $260,000.David Anthony Sanchez, 36, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.Federal prosecutors said Sanchez, who also went by "Dave the Jewler," "Rueben Alexis De Jesus Santana" and other aliases, impersonated online streamer N3ON to convince organizers of a cryptocurrency memecoin project that the streamer had agreed to endorse and participate in it.According to court records, Sanchez created online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3ON and communicated with the project's organizers while posing as both the streamer and his representative.Prosecutors said Sanchez also executed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent organizers an AI-generated voice recording that mimicked the streamer's voice to falsely confirm his participation.Believing the representations were legitimate, the victims transferred approximately $260,000 in cryptocurrency to accounts controlled by Sanchez, according to prosecutors.Authorities said Sanchez later converted a substantial portion of the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to conceal the source and ownership of the money. Prosecutors said he used the proceeds for his personal benefit."Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm," Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in the release. She said Sanchez exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate victims' trust and take their money.In addition to his 47-month prison sentence, Sanchez was ordered to pay restitution to the victims. The amount of restitution was not specified in the release.The FBI's Miami Field Office investigated the case.

A new holiday tradition is taking root at the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, where Luminary Nights will bring holiday lights, nighttime lighthouse climbs, local music and shopping to the historic waterfront property in December.The limited event is scheduled for Dec. 11, 12, 18, and 19. Christmas and the holidays have taken over Nieko’s Neighborhood Bar in Jupiter’s Abacoa Town Center, where nearly every corner has been transformed with holiday decorations, seasonal drinks, and family activities. The celebration is also being used to collect toys for three local charities.The family behind Nieko’s said they wanted to create an immersive Christmas experience that visitors would notice as soon as they walked through the door.“We wanted a really fun holiday Christmas bar that people would walk in the door and just feel Christmas right in their face, like, 'OK, this is amazing,'” said Nieko Tischler, Owner, Nieko’s Neighborhood Bar.For the transformation, the family tackled the restaurant one section at a time.“My family, my husband, my cousin, and myself, we pretty much just went through each part of the restaurant and we wanted it to feel like an awesome fun Christmas bar,” Nieko said.Christmas activities for kids in AbacoaThe holiday experience isn’t limited to adults.Children visiting the dining room can write letters to Santa and put them into a special Santa letter dropbox.The bar also serves hot chocolate with a chocolate spoon and s’mores stick.The idea is to give families another way to enjoy the Christmas atmosphere together while visiting Abacoa Town Center during the holiday season.Christmas cocktails fill the menu. “We’re doing the Oasis Project, Chasing a Dream, and Little Smiles, and from now until Christmas, if you bring an unwrapped toy, you get a free drink on us.”The toy drive adds a giving component to Nieko’s holiday transformation at a time when families and organizations across South Florida are collecting gifts for children ahead of Christmas.For Nieko’s, the result is a holiday destination built around decorations, food, drinks, and family activities, with a chance for visitors to help children in the community at the same time.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved $200,000 to fund a study that will analyze water movement during the recent flooding in Jensen Beach and identify ways to reduce future flood risks. Floodwaters earlier this month left homes and roads underwater in parts of Jensen Beach. The study will examine how water moved through the Savannas Preserve area during the storm, as some residents have questioned whether water discharged into the Blackwell Reservoir, which drains into the Savannas Preserve, contributed to the flooding. "What's happening now is not going to stop. This is an El Niño event that we are in through April. It's going to come and go," resident Jacqui Thurlow-Lippisch said during the Nov. 17 county commissioner meeting. Public Works Director James Gorton says the hydraulic model funded by the county will focus on two main objectives. "First one is model the storm event that we just had. We need to update, get some of the development that has occurred to our north, put into that model first and then model that storm, see where the weaknesses were, and then secondarily look at some solutions to reduce the risk," Gorton said. This initiative follows a separate study conducted by the county to analyze areas that have repeatedly flooded, aiming to understand the causes and identify potential solutions. Engineering permit manager and floodplain coordinator Christine Madsen said the analysis identified 53 repetitive loss areas. "We determined what some of the potential causes of the flooding were, and we used it to identify different projects that we could take and move forward within the future," Madsen said. One photo from the study shows flooding in the St. Lucie Settlement area along SW Salerno Road, where eight homes were elevated above the 100-year flood elevation with assistance from FEMA. Another photo shows one of the completed homes. "Flood losses are terrible. Just 1 inch of water can majorly impact a property. I mean it can cause up to $25,000 worth of damage," Madsen said. "We want to do whatever we can to help them." Residents can review the analysis on the county's website. Those with questions can call the county at 772-288-5956.

Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

Thousands of Port St. Lucie residents can put away their pots after city officials lifted a precautionary boil water notice Saturday afternoon. The City of Port St. Lucie announced the all-clear at 3:15 p.m. Saturday after water quality tests confirmed the water was safe to drink. The notice affected approximately 21,000 customers in Tradition and areas west of Interstate 95 following a water main break Tuesday near Glades Cut Off Road. See also: A helping of hope: 600 turkeys bring Thanksgiving cheer to South Florida families Residents in the following communities no longer need to boil their water: Tradition Western Grove Riverland Wilson Grove Southern Grove Copper Creek Wylder Verano The affected area stretched west of I-95 south to Becker Road, including communities along Glades Cut Off Road. According to city officials, the break occurred when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main. City crews responded immediately and completed repairs within hours. Flushing and required water quality testing followed. After tests confirmed the water was safe, officials lifted the precautionary notice. The city thanked the roughly 21,000 affected customers for their patience throughout the disruption.

St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan during their Dec. 1 meeting. County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan at the meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Commissioners can ask questions and approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update builds on the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft on Aug. 11. The plan is intended to guide future development and help the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. Among the long-term opportunities in the draft is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. As CBS12 previously reported, the proposed facility could position Fort Pierce to support recovery work tied to Florida’s growing space industry . The plan describes it as one part of a broader working waterfront vision, alongside mega-yacht services, marine research and workforce training, recreation and public access. The rocket-recovery proposal is one part of a broader vision for the Port of Fort Pierce as a mixed-use working waterfront. The plan also outlines Harbour Pointe as a public-facing district, with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also envisions a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. It calls for continued growth of the port’s mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, as well as a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service. The plan includes infrastructure and access projects, such as a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements and a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail. It also proposes a future Port to Park link to improve access between the waterfront and Franklin Park. See also: 3 auto insurers directed to refund $122 million in excess profits to Florida customers The 2026 update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan rather than replacing it. The document lays out a long-term vision for development; proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion. The county says commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft plan on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage .

Frances Bertino has lived on Lakehurst Drive for nearly 30 years. For the past three weeks, a hole in the road outside her home has kept her from making the right turn out of her driveway. "I've been here since 1996 when we built the house," Bertino said. "I never had any problems until that. Until now." The hole is about five feet wide and sits in the middle of the road. It opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. The City of Port St. Lucie's flooded streets dashboard lists Lakehurst Drive between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street as "closed indefinitely due to infrastructure damage." Bertino said that when the road first closed, the barricades blocked her driveway. "They said if I got out of it, I was going to get arrested," she said. "I couldn't sleep at night thinking I'm landlocked." The barricades were later moved back. Now she turns around and drives out the other way. It seems funny at first," she said. Her neighbor, who often gives her rides, has had to change how he gets in and out. "Now he pulls in the driveway, now backs up and pulls out." See also: Travelers pack DJT airport ahead of Thanksgiving amid jitters over recent outages Bertino said she reported the damage to the city and was told a water pipe was involved. Asked whether she had heard anything since, she said, "No, I have heard nothing." On Wednesday afternoon, while CBS12 was interviewing her, city crews arrived to inspect the hole. "This is the first time they've been out to inspect it that I know of, because I didn't see anybody here," Bertino said. Three weeks." Asked whether the inspection gave her confidence the road would be fixed soon, she said, "I hope so." City spokesperson Scott Samples said a temporary fix for Lakehurst Drive is expected sometime next week. "The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes," Samples said. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city, and two are still closed. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. He said crews decide which roads to fix first based on how bad the damage is and how many people depend on that road. He said the repeated rain has slowed the work. Wednesday's Flood Watch is the third the city has prepared for since the start of the month. "This kind of weather makes it harder to continue to do those kinds of repairs," Samples said. He said supplies are another problem. Flooding up and down Florida's east coast has put many communities in need of the same repair materials at once. "A lot of those materials that we require to be able to fix those roads, it makes it harder to obtain those," he said. The storm also filled the swale outside her home. Bertino said she had seen water that high only once before, during Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in 2004. "It was all the way to the top. I could not believe it," she said. "We're talking about Frances and Jeanne. And this is just a storm." Lakehurst Drive is one of two streets the city lists as closed indefinitely for infrastructure damage. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. The closures come as federal help begins to reach the region. President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a Major Disaster Declaration for the flooding that began Oct. 31. That makes FEMA individual assistance available to residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs, and uninsured property losses. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. The declaration does not yet cover St. Lucie County's local governments. Five of the six counties were also approved for FEMA public assistance, which pays local governments back for debris removal and emergency work. St. Lucie County was not on that list. The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters say 1 to 3 inches of rain is most likely, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some spots. They warn that heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

Health officials are warning swimmers to avoid water-related activities at several locations along the Treasure Coast due to elevated bacteria levels following recent heavy rain and flooding. Jetty Park Beach in Fort Pierce is among the affected areas, where advisory signs have been posted to alert visitors. "Heavy amounts of rain that we've experienced here in St. Lucie County, really here on the Treasure Coast, have resulted in higher bacteria levels in our waterways," Erick Gill, Communications Director at St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners said. The Florida Department of Health reported that tests conducted Monday revealed enterococcus bacteria levels exceeding state guidelines at eight locations in St. Lucie County and three in Martin County. "A lot of it is the heavy rainfall and the runoff that we're getting, and agricultural as well as some septic tanks that may have been impacted by the amount of rain and flooding that we've gotten over the last couple of weeks," Gill said. Health officials are advising against swimming and other water-related activities at the affected locations due to an increased risk of illness. For some beach visitors, like Enma Kennedy, the advisories are not a deterrent to enjoying the scenery. "We get to enjoy it regardless of what's going. We have family that just flew in yesterday from California, their first time here, and look where we are. Rather rain or shine, we're here," Kennedy said. In St. Lucie County, advisories remain in effect at Jetty Park Beach, South Beach Causeway, Little Jim Bridge, Jaycee Park, Surfside Park, Walton Rocks Beach, Blue Heron, and Frederick Douglass Memorial Park. Health officials said the advisories will remain in place until bacteria levels fall below accepted health standards. Gill is also warning everyone to be look out for fire ants. "In addition to the bacteria levels residents should be aware that there are a lot of fire ants out there and other wildlife out there that might be seeking drier grounds so be cautious, when you're out hiking or playing in the back yard because fire ants are seeking shelter as well," Gill said. A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Lucie. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem. hero.headline: Deputies seek help identifying suspects in Lakewood Park overnight vehicle burglaries
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is investigating multiple overnight vehicle burglaries in Lakewood Park and asking for help identifying people shown in surveillance footage and photos involving a stolen credit card.

The burglaries were reported along Lakeland Boulevard, North Boulevard, Coquina Boulevard, Deleon Avenue and Paso Robles Boulevard, deputies said. Surveillance footage from one location shows two people walking onto a driveway, opening unlocked car doors and entering vehicles. Photos released by the sheriff’s office show suspects using a credit card stolen during the burglaries. One image shows what a suspect wore during the incidents, according to the agency.

Anyone who recognizes the people in the video or photos, or has information about the burglaries, is asked to call the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at 772-462-7300. The agency recommends removing valuables and keys from vehicles and locking car doors.
hero.article_text: The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is investigating multiple overnight vehicle burglaries in the Lakewood Park area after surveillance video showed two people entering unlocked cars. The incidents were reported along Lakeland Boulevard, North Boulevard, Coquina Boulevard, Deleon Avenue and Paso Robles Boulevard, deputies said. Surveillance footage from one location shows two people walking onto a driveway, opening unlocked car doors and entering vehicles. The sheriff’s office said there were no broken windows or signs of forced entry. Photos released by the agency show suspects using a credit card stolen during the burglaries. One image shows what a suspect was wearing during the incidents, according to the sheriff’s office. hero.headline: Martin County approves $200,000 study of Jensen Beach flooding and future risks
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners unanimously approved $200,000 for a study to model the recent flooding in Jensen Beach and identify ways to reduce future flood risks. The study will examine how water moved through the Savannas Preserve area during the storm, which left homes and roads underwater in parts of Jensen Beach earlier this month.

Some residents have questioned whether water discharged into the Blackwell Reservoir, which drains into the Savannas Preserve, contributed to the flooding. Public Works Director James Gorton said the county-funded hydraulic model will have two main objectives: reconstructing the recent storm event and examining potential solutions to reduce flood risk. Before modeling the storm, the county will update the model to account for development to the north, Gorton said. The work will help identify weaknesses during the storm.

The initiative follows a separate county study of areas that have repeatedly flooded. Engineering permit manager and floodplain coordinator Christine Madsen said that analysis identified 53 repetitive loss areas. “We determined what some of the potential causes of the flooding were, and we used it to identify different projects that we could take and move forward within the future,” Madsen said.

The earlier study includes a photo of flooding in the St. Lucie Settlement area along SW Salerno Road, where eight homes were elevated above the 100-year flood elevation with assistance from FEMA. Another photo shows one of the completed homes. “Flood losses are terrible. Just 1 inch of water can majorly impact a property. I mean it can cause up to $25,000 worth of damage,” Madsen said.

Residents can review the analysis of repeatedly flooded areas on the county’s website. Those with questions can call the county at 772-288-5956.

Martin County Utilities said it has since implemented additional training and safeguards within its data collection software.

hero.headline: Four arrested after alleged attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club
hero.body:
Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, were arrested after an alleged attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The agency is asking residents to review security footage and check their homes and vehicles as investigators determine whether other properties were targeted.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when a family's 17-year-old son heard a suspicious noise outside the home and alerted his parents. The family reviewed security footage and noticed one camera was not working properly. Looking back through earlier recordings, they saw three people circling the house, Budensiek said. Video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door, blocking its view. The family called 911.

Investigators said the group had parked near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community. Deputies checked a parking lot near the canal and found a vehicle. One person was taken into custody near it, while the others fled, according to the sheriff. Deputies established a perimeter and searched with help from aviation units, K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Two suspects were found hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal. Budensiek said they were the last two apprehended after the extensive overnight search.

The adults arrested were identified as Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and Cameron Elijah Mapson, all 21. A 16-year-old was also arrested. All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to the sheriff's office. Wise also faces charges of grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. Investigators recovered masks, gloves and a stolen handgun with an extended magazine. Budensiek said the handgun was found as investigators retraced the route between the vehicle and the family's home.

Investigators are examining digital evidence to establish why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Palm City. Residents who discover missing property or signs of a break-in are asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie expects temporary Lakehurst Drive repair next week after flood damage
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie expects a temporary repair to Lakehurst Drive sometime next week, three weeks after flooding opened a hole in the road. Two city streets remain closed indefinitely because of infrastructure damage, and repeated rain and shortages of repair materials have slowed the work, city spokesperson Scott Samples said.

Lakehurst Drive is closed between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street. The other closure is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city. Crews prioritize repairs based on the severity of the damage and how many people depend on each road.

The hole on Lakehurst Drive is about five feet wide and opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. Frances Bertino, who has lived on the street for nearly 30 years, said it has kept her from turning right out of her driveway for three weeks. Barricades initially blocked her driveway but were later moved back. She now turns around and drives out the other way. City crews arrived Wednesday afternoon to inspect the hole.

“The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes,” Samples said.

Wednesday’s Flood Watch was the third the city had prepared for since the start of the month. Samples said flooding along Florida’s east coast has left many communities seeking the same repair materials at once, making supplies harder to obtain.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters expect 1 to 3 inches of rain, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some places. Heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

President Donald Trump approved Florida’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration for flooding that began Oct. 31, making FEMA individual assistance available in St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs and uninsured property losses. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man gets 47 months in prison for $260K AI cryptocurrency fraud
hero.body:
David Anthony Sanchez, 36, of Port St. Lucie, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison and ordered to pay restitution for a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that used an AI-generated voice to impersonate online streamer N3ON and cost victims about $260,000. Sanchez pleaded guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Federal prosecutors said Sanchez convinced organizers of a cryptocurrency memecoin project that N3ON had agreed to endorse and participate in it. According to court records, Sanchez created online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3ON and communicated with organizers while posing as both the streamer and his representative. He also executed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent organizers an AI-generated recording that mimicked the streamer's voice to falsely confirm his participation, prosecutors said.

Believing those representations were legitimate, the victims transferred approximately $260,000 in cryptocurrency to accounts Sanchez controlled, according to prosecutors. Authorities said he then converted a substantial portion of the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to conceal the money's source and ownership. Prosecutors said Sanchez used the proceeds for his personal benefit.

“Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm,” Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in a release. She said Sanchez exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate victims' trust and take their money. The FBI's Miami Field Office investigated the case.
